criterion_notes.c1: Examines household access to domestic water supply (public treated water supply, developer boreholes, individual wells/boreholes, and water vendors) and sanitation services (water closet toilets with septic tanks and soak away pits, domestic refuse bins, and storm-water drainage) alongside electricity and neighbourhood facilities in nine urban public housing estates in Ogun State.
criterion_notes.c2: PASSES PLAIN WORDING (borderline) / FAILS NARROW 2026-10-13 RULE-TYPE READING. Under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2 ('Examines a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), the paper can be read as evaluating institutional public-housing delivery by Ogun State government housing agencies and private-sector partners under Nigeria's post-2002 New National Housing and Urban Development Policy (NNHUDP) reforms (attributing 3% public water coverage to Ogun State Water Corporation inefficiency and lack of inter-agency coordination with public housing providers), which would lead to inclusion under a broad institutional-programme reading (though borderline even on plain wording because all nine estates are pooled descriptively with no institutional variable measured or compared). Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is clearly NOT met: the empirical study focuses exclusively on physical/spatial accessibility and post-occupancy satisfaction with generic public-housing project delivery, while the historical overview of housing policies, PPPs, and state corporations serves solely as unanalysed macro-governance background. No rule-type mechanism directly governing water or sanitation access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, discretion, or utility ownership/regulatory rules) is empirically analysed (even respondent tenure status is reported only as a sample demographic in Table 1 and never linked to water or sanitation outcomes).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical data from a structured household questionnaire administered to 452 household heads (out of 670 sampled occupied housing units across nine public housing estates) and a field observation schedule conducted between December 2009 and February 2010.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports quantitative descriptive outcomes for household water source availability (3% public water supply / 97% without treated water in residences; 46% boreholes built by housing providers; 25.8% water vendors; 25.2% individual wells/boreholes), human waste and solid waste sanitation access (100% water closet toilets with functional septic tanks and soak away pits; 35% access to refuse bins), and mean 5-point Likert satisfaction scores for water supply (2.18) and drainage facilities (2.83).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (452 household heads / occupied dwelling units across nine urban public housing estates in Ogun State), focal condition (residence in newly constructed public housing schemes delivered between 2003 and 2010, though lacking an eligible rule-type exposure), water/sanitation outcomes, and study design (cross-sectional household survey and observation schedule) are clearly identifiable.

evidence_quotes.quote: It was observed that although the majority of households in the housing estates have good access to human waste disposal system, accessibility to refuse bins, treated water, electricity, and public transport services as well as educational, shopping, recreational, healthcare, drainage, and other vital facilities is poor.

Indeed, Doi, Kii, and Nakanishi (2008) observed that there are different aspects of accessibility often considered by researchers. These include physical, mental, economic, and financial accessibility. In this study, the focus is on physical accessibility.

In the current study, we adopted physical availability of services and facilities and satisfaction with the quality of services and the distance between their dwelling units and facilities in evaluating the accessibility to services and facilities for residents in public housing in urban areas of Ogun State.

This paper draws on a study conducted to evaluate the overall performance of public housing in Ogun State. The study was based on a survey research method and data were derived mainly through household surveys and observation conducted between December 2009 and February 2010 in the study area.
The study also found that all the housing units sampled have water closet type of toilets with functional septic tanks and soak away pits for the collection of human waste and foul water.

Interesting, only 3 % of the respondents indicated that public water supply system was their main source of water. This result clearly shows that the majority (97 %) of the households from where the respondents were drawn from do not have access to treated water in their residences.

raw_response.exposure: Residence in newly constructed public housing schemes delivered by Ogun State government housing agencies and private sector partners (2003–2010) — generic public-housing project delivery and physical/spatial proximity of amenities (no legal, administrative, or rule-type governance mechanism analysed)
raw_response.outcome: Household water and sanitation access and satisfaction: main domestic water supply source (46% boreholes built by housing providers, 25.8% water vendors, 25.2% individual wells and boreholes, 3% public water supply / 97% lacking treated water), sanitation facilities (100% water closet toilets with septic tanks and soak away pits; 35% access to refuse bins), and mean 5-point Likert satisfaction scores for water supply (2.18) and drainage facilities (2.83)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Household heads in nine completed and occupied public housing estates built between 2003 and 2010 in urban areas of Ogun State (Abeokuta, Ijebu-Ode, Ota, Agbara, and Ibafo-Gateway City); stratified sample of 670 occupied housing units (from 709 occupied out of 1,523 completed units), yielding 452 valid household questionnaires
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). While the paper empirically measures household access to water supply and sanitation facilities across nine newly constructed public housing estates in urban Ogun State (N=452 households), it is a descriptive post-occupancy evaluation of physical/spatial accessibility and generic public-housing project delivery. Historical discussion of Nigerian housing agencies, the Ogun State Water Corporation, and the 2002 New National Housing and Urban Development Policy (NNHUDP) provides only unanalysed macro-governance background, and all nine estates are pooled into univariate descriptive statistics without examining any rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance mechanism (such as eligibility rules, tenure/documentation requirements, tariffs, discretion, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure) governing water or sanitation access. Under a broad/plain reading of Criterion 2, evaluating state/PPP public-housing programme delivery would pass as an institutional delivery factor, so plain_criterion2_decision is recorded as 'include'.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional household survey (structured questionnaire) and field observation schedule
